stops.name: Buenos Aires, casa natal, calle Santo Domingo
stops.campa: On the third of June, in the merchant house of Domingo Belgrano Peri on the street of Santo Domingo, a son is born to the Ligurian trader and to María Josefa González Casero, criolla of Santiago del Estero. The bells of the nearby convent ring the hour over the flat-roofed city on the estuary. The child is christened Manuel José Joaquín del Corazón de Jesús: the heart of Jesus set into his name like a seed, for a life that will be spent and emptied for the land he is born into.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Catedral, bautismo
stops.campa: One day old, the child is carried the two blocks to the Cathedral of the Most Holy Trinity and baptized at its font. The water is poured, the long name pronounced, the godparents answer for him. Outside, carts creak toward the Plaza Mayor and the river wind comes up the barrancas. The parish book takes the entry in a clerk's brown ink: the first document of a life that will end, fifty years later almost to the day, a few streets from this font.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Real Colegio de San Carlos
stops.campa: The boy walks each morning to the Real Colegio de San Carlos in the manzana of the old Jesuit block, where Latin, logic and philosophy are beaten into the sons of the city. He is quick, orderly, grave beyond his years. The masters mark him for letters, his father marks him for something larger than the counting-house. In these cold classrooms the criollo learns the grammar of an empire he will one day unmake, courteously, in perfect Castilian.

stops.name: Salamanca, la Universidad
stops.campa: Sent across the ocean with his brother Francisco, the young porteño matriculates in laws at Salamanca, the honey-stoned mother of universities. But the frog on the carved skull of the facade watches a student whose true syllabus is elsewhere, living languages, political economy, public law: Campomanes, Jovellanos, the physiocrats. In the tertulias he hears Spain's own enlightened men doubt the old order aloud. The law student is quietly becoming an economist of a country that does not yet exist.
stops.quote: Confieso que mi aplicación no la contraje tanto a la carrera que fui a emprender, como al estudio de los idiomas vivos, de la economía política y del derecho público.

stops.name: Valladolid, la Chancillería, bachiller en leyes
stops.campa: At Valladolid he takes his bachelor's degree in laws and license to practice before the royal Chancillería. It is the year the world turns: across the Pyrenees the Bastille falls, and the shockwave runs through every lecture hall and salon in Spain. The men of letters he moves among catch fire, and so does he. Liberty, equality, security, property: the words enter him like a creed received, and he begins to see tyrants wherever these rights are denied.
stops.quote: Se apoderaron de mí las ideas de libertad, igualdad, seguridad, propiedad, y sólo veía tiranos en los que se oponían a que el hombre, fuese donde fuese, no disfrutase de unos derechos que Dios y la naturaleza le habían concedido.

stops.name: Madrid, la licencia papal y la Secretaría del Consulado
stops.campa: In Madrid the young lawyer obtains from Pope Pius VI a dispensation to read the forbidden books: the condemned philosophers pass legally into his hands, sealed with the fisherman's ring. He is elected president of the academy of practicing lawyers; and in 1793 the Crown, wanting enlightened criollos for its new commercial tribunals, names him perpetual secretary of the Consulado to be erected in Buenos Aires. He sails home carrying banned ideas with papal permission and a royal commission to apply them.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, primera sesión del Consulado
stops.campa: On 2 June 1794 the Consulado of Buenos Aires holds its first session with Belgrano, twenty-four years old, as its perpetual secretary. He comes armed with Adam Smith and the physiocrats; he finds a room of monopolist merchants. Year after year his annual memorias preach agriculture, industry, commerce, roads, the education of women, free schools for the poor: seeds thrown on the stony ground of the colonial order, and remembered later as the first economic program of the nation.
stops.quote: No sabían más que su comercio monopolista, a saber: comprar por cuatro para vender por ocho.
stops.quote_source: Autobiografía de Manuel Belgrano (1814), on the merchants of the Consulado

stops.name: Buenos Aires, fundación de la Escuela de Náutica
stops.campa: From the secretary's desk he founds schools the way other men build fortunes: on 25 November 1799 the Escuela de Náutica opens under the Consulado's wing, and with it an Academy of Geometry and Drawing. Pilots for the rivers, draftsmen for the workshops: a country trained into existence. The Crown, suspicious of educated colonials, will later order the schools closed; Belgrano records the wound and keeps sowing. Education is already his fixed idea: without it, he writes, we shall never be more than we sadly are.
stops.quote: Uno de los principales medios que se deben adoptar a este fin son las escuelas gratuitas, donde puedan los infelices mandar a sus hijos.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, entrada de los ingleses
stops.campa: On 27 June 1806 Beresford's redcoats march into the undefended city and the viceroy flees. Belgrano, captain of urban militia who has never learned war, watches the enemy column enter the Plaza and feels the shame of it enter his bones like iron. In that indignation the soldier is conceived: the civilian economist who will teach himself armies. Ordered to swear allegiance to the British Crown, he refuses outright and rides for the ferry rather than bend.
stops.quote: Confieso que me indigné, y que nunca sentí más no saber ni aun los rudimentos de la milicia.

stops.name: Montevideo, el destierro voluntario
stops.campa: Rather than swear to the King of England, Belgrano crosses to the Banda Oriental. In Montevideo and the villages of the other shore he waits out the occupation among emigrés, hearing the news from the captive city and sharpening a conviction that will steer his whole politics: dominion may pass, but not to a new master. The old king or none, and in the hollow of that 'none', unspoken yet, the patria already stirs.
stops.quote: O el amo viejo, o ninguno.
stops.quote_source: Dictum attributed to Belgrano during the English invasions, recorded in the patriotic tradition (cf. Autobiografía)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, la Reconquista
stops.campa: On 12 August 1806 Liniers retakes the city street by street and the people discover, with astonishment that never quite fades, that they defended themselves without Spain. Belgrano returns to a Buenos Aires in arms and takes his place in the new criollo militias, elected sargento mayor of the Regiment of Patricios. He drills in the plazas with a manual in one hand, learning at thirty-six the trade he was too indignant not to learn. The city has tasted its own strength; so has he.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, la Defensa
stops.campa: Whitelocke comes back in 1807 with ten thousand men and the city swallows them whole. From the flat rooftops boiling water, grapeshot and musketry pour into the packed columns; the streets south of the Plaza become a trap of a hundred ambushes. Belgrano serves through the Defensa with the Patricios, and watches an imperial army surrender to armed vecinos. The lesson enters the canon: this people, armed and resolved, can defeat anyone. Three years later it will remember.
